1bbab8a355cb560f46fe9beb.title_original: Braid: Sybil-Resistant Decentralized Identity with Trustless Key Recovery and Non-Transferable Anonymous Credentials
1bbab8a355cb560f46fe9beb.excerpt: arXiv:2307.14679v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Decentralized identity frameworks grant users full sovereignty over their digital assets in the Web3 ecosystem. However, allowing arbitrary creation of identifiers makes the system susceptible to Sybil attacks and puts assets at risk when keys are lost or compromised. Moreover, the lack of identification prevents anonymous credential schemes from deterring malicious transfers. Existing solutions link identifiers to entities through trusted intermediaries, which are not always accessible and require costly offline interactions. We introduce Braid, a decentralized identity system with Sybil resistance, trustless key recovery, and non-transferable anonymous credentials. Braid creates blockchain-based bindings between identifiers and gradually combines identifiers belonging to the same holder into a unified associated identifier. As all identifiers within an association are presumed to belong to one individual, any fraudulent activity can be detected. The association grows larger as interactions increase, substantially reducing the likelihood of successful Sybil attacks. This mechanism allows holders to recover identifiers with lost keys or partial key compromise by proving knowledge of specific association structures. Additionally, Braid prevents unauthorized transfers through blockchain-based identifier-key bindings and proofs of ownership for credentials. Compared with representative prior approaches that provide only campaig

2f4207a28a42996f3dfe4987.title_original: On the Vulnerability of Lane Detectors to Physical Shadow Attack
2f4207a28a42996f3dfe4987.excerpt: arXiv:2409.18248v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Automated Lane Centering (ALC) systems are critical components of Level 2 autonomous vehicles, yet their reliance on Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) for lane detection introduces security vulnerabilities. This work introduces the Negative Shadow (NS) Attack, a novel physical-world adversarial technique that exploits intensity bias in shadow-removal preprocessing, where bright patches within shadowed regions are misclassified as genuine lane markings. Unlike previous attacks requiring illegal road markings, the NS attack is passive and stealthy, utilizing sunlight filtered through shaped occluders placed on private property to cast patterns onto the roadway. We utilize a genetic algorithm to optimize the geometry of these shadows against three state-of-the-art lane detection systems: CLRerNet, HybridNets, and TwinLiteNet. The attack is evaluated across three hazard scenarios -- left-turn deviation, head-on collision, and off-road deviation -- using software-in-the-loop simulations with CARLA-OpenPilot, which demonstrated violation rates of up to 100%. Further validation is provided through a miniature road testbed and a real-world deployment where the attack successfully caused a Comma 3X-equipped vehicle to depart its lane. Additionally, a human-subject study indicates high stealth, with 83.6% of participants failing to detect the adversarial patterns, and an assessment of input-preprocessing defenses shows they offer only limit

fcf407316a5044a7e9668242.title_original: Understanding Help Seeking for Digital Privacy, Safety, and Security on Reddit
fcf407316a5044a7e9668242.excerpt: arXiv:2601.11398v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The complexity of navigating digital privacy, safety, and security threats often falls directly on users. This leads to users seeking help from family and peers, platforms and advice guides, dedicated communities, and even large language models (LLMs). As a precursor to improving resources across this ecosystem, our community needs to understand what help seeking looks like in the wild. To that end, we build a scaled analysis pipeline leveraging LLMs to sift through over two billion Reddit posts from the last five years to identify where and for what users seek digital privacy, safety, or security help. We isolate four million relevant posts with 93% precision and recall and automatically annotate each with the topics discussed (e.g., privacy configurations, data misuse, account compromise, and more). We use this dataset to understand the scope and scale of help seeking on Reddit, the subcommunities that provide help, and to qualitatively analyze the types of help sought. Our work informs the development of better resources for users (e.g., user guides or LLM help-giving agents) while underscoring the inherent challenges of supporting users through complex combinations of threats, platforms, mitigations, context, and emotions.

38186c7bc5f639bd497694ed.title_original: Triosecuris: Formally Verified Protection Against Speculative Control-Flow Hijacking
38186c7bc5f639bd497694ed.excerpt: arXiv:2601.22978v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper introduces Triosecuris, a formally verified defense against Spectre BTB, RSB, and PHT that combines CET-style hardware-assisted control-flow integrity with compiler-inserted speculative load hardening (SLH). Triosecuris is based on the novel observation that in the presence of CET-style protection, we can precisely detect BTB misspeculation for indirect calls and RSB misspeculation for returns and set the SLH misspeculation flag. We formalize Triosecuris as a transformation in Rocq and provide a machine-checked proof that it achieves relative security: any transformed program running with speculation leaks no more than what the source program leaks without speculation. This strong security guarantee applies to arbitrary programs, even those not following the cryptographic constant-time programming discipline.

216a10d2857b05a6647629bb.title_original: SST-Guard: Detecting and Characterizing Server-Side Google Analytics in the Wild
216a10d2857b05a6647629bb.excerpt: arXiv:2604.27497v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: As web browsers increasingly implement anti-tracking features, the web tracking ecosystem has been shifting from the client-side to the server-side. Instead of sending requests directly to the tracker's endpoint, server-side tracking (SST) sends tracking requests to publisher-controlled or intermediary endpoints that then forward the information to trackers from the server-side. As a result, client-side tracking protections are becoming fragile because direct client-to-tracker requests may no longer be observed. In this paper, we investigate the server-side Google Analytics (sGA), the most widely deployed third-party tracking service on the web today. We present SST-GUARD, a multi-modal browser-based approach for detecting sGA. The key insight behind SST-GUARD is that common sGA deployments change the standard Google Analytics endpoints, but still leave semantic artifacts of data collection by Google Analytics in the browser, including identifiers, event metadata, cookies, and JavaScript state. SST-GUARD detects these artifacts using value-templates, which use regular expressions to match semantic value patterns across multiple modalities: network requests, cookies, and the window object, providing robustness against obfuscation of one modality. We validate SST-GUARD on Tranco top-10k websites, detecting 4.0% (401) sGA domains with over 93.0% accuracy across three modalities, with network request classifier demonstrating the

96f93e4542223004f9358004.title_original: Cross-Modal Backdoor Attack on Connector-based Multimodal Large Language Models
96f93e4542223004f9358004.excerpt: arXiv:2605.07490v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Assembling multimodal large language models (MLLMs) from pretrained components has become a widely adopted practice in the open-source ecosystem, yet the supply-chain risks of lightweight connectors remain largely unexplored. We propose a cross-modal backdoor attack that exploits this gap. By poisoning only the connector with a single seed sample and a small set of augmented variants from one modality, the adversary establishes a compact malicious region in the shared latent space associated with a target output. A centroid extracted from this region then serves as a latent anchor for cross-modal activation: adversarial inputs from any other modality can be optimized offline to reach this anchor, triggering the target response without access to the deployed model. Evaluations on PandaGPT and NExT-GPT show same-modality attack success rates (ASR) up to 99.9%, with most cross-modal settings exceeding 95.0% ASR under bounded perturbations. Experiments on ChatBridge further demonstrate the attack's effectiveness across different connector architectures. The attack produces 0.0% backdoor leakage on clean inputs and maintains weight-cosine similarity above 0.97 relative to benign connectors. Existing defenses fail to neutralize the threat without substantial utility degradation, revealing that a single poisoned connector can establish a reusable backdoor pathway across modalities.

19d56a0830091dae4025a3cf.title_original: No Country for Old Privacy: The Evolving Challenges of Anonymity in Bitcoin
19d56a0830091dae4025a3cf.excerpt: arXiv:2607.00772v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present a longitudinal measurement study on the adoption of detectable, second-generation anonymisation protocols in the Bitcoin network, including CoinJoin, CoinSwap, CoinShuffle and Stealth Addresses. By implementing and refining a suite of heuristic filters, we identify over 5 million candidate CoinJoin and 23.3 million candidate CoinSwap transactions. Notably, the use of CoinShuffle was unexpectedly found to be closely aligned with the operation of coordinator-based CoinJoin services such as Wasabi and Whirlpool. Our analysis reveals consistently low adoption rates, with these protocols typically constituting less than 1% of network transactions, and a sharp decline in detectable usage following key regulatory events. Furthermore, we find no evidence of standardised Stealth Address adoption, indicating a failure to converge on a common privacy standard. This study provides a comprehensive picture of a niche ecosystem whose on-chain visibility has been largely suppressed, strongly suggesting the migration of privacy-seeking users to less transparent and less detectable methods.

696abb3b15ac055f6fb1a921.title_original: ROPE: Routed Origin Policy Enforcement against Indirect Prompt Injection
696abb3b15ac055f6fb1a921.excerpt: arXiv:2608.27496v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Tool-using LLM agents execute consequential operations on behalf of users. Because the LLM driving an agent processes trusted user instructions and untrusted content in the same context, agents are vulnerable to indirect prompt injection attacks that induce unintended actions by mixing malicious instructions into benign data. Defenses based on prompting or content detection are easily evaded by paraphrasing attacks, while system-level defenses that constrain tool calls using inferred user intent, or restrict which sources can supply values to sensitive tools, greatly compromise utility. We present ROPE (Routed Origin Policy Enforcement), a defense that greatly improves the utility-security tradeoff by leveraging system roots of trust to create and enforce per-task policies on sensitive tool parameters. Our key insight is that authentication and integrity protection provide a basis for identifying the source of content independently of instructions embedded in it. Before a task unfolds, an LLM router reads only trusted task input to set a provenance rule for each sensitive tool parameter, accounting for the nature of the task and the values and sources the user specified. As the agent works, an origin labeler records where each piece of content came from, using the user's request, platform metadata, and protected record fields as trust anchors. Before any sensitive tool executes, a deterministic verifier requires each of its

921afeedd26ba01d5a421e22.title_original: GPUThor: Amplifying Rowhammer Attacks via Non-Uniform Patterns to Exploit ECC-Protected GPUs
921afeedd26ba01d5a421e22.excerpt: arXiv:2609.16546v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: GDDR memory in GPUs is vulnerable to Rowhammer attacks, where rapid memory accesses induce bit flips in adjacent cells, enabling data tampering and privilege escalation. However, prior GPU Rowhammer attacks trigger only tens to hundreds of bit flips, orders of magnitude fewer than CPU attacks, severely limiting their practical impact. This gap stems from the reliance of existing GPU Rowhammer attacks on uniform hammering patterns that activate aggressor and decoy rows equally, which results in low hammering intensity for aggressor rows. We present GPUThor, a high-intensity Rowhammer attack on NVIDIA GPUs leveraging non-uniform hammering. GPUThor reverse engineers GPU memory-access coalescing behavior to enable non-uniform hammering patterns on GPUs, that activate aggressor rows more intensely than decoy rows. Additionally, by identifying refresh instances when in-DRAM mitigations are applied, it constructs longer attack patterns that escape mitigation across refresh intervals, further increasing hammering intensity. Together, these techniques yield 500X to 23,500X more bit flips than prior GPU Rowhammer attacks, across several NVIDIA GPUs (A4000, A4500, A5000, A6000), reaching bit flip rates close to state-of-the-art CPU Rowhammer attacks. GPUThor also enables the first Rowhammer exploits on ECC-protected GPUs, inducing uncorrectable double and triple bit flips, making denial-of-service and privilege-escalation attacks pract

900841249178d2873a77fc20.title_original: HDKEM: Authentication Allocation for Deniable Hybrid Key Exchange
900841249178d2873a77fc20.excerpt: arXiv:2610.16100v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A deniable authenticated key exchange (DAKE) establishes an authenticated shared key without giving third parties proof of participation. Post-quantum DAKEs use ring signatures, message authentication codes, or split key-encapsulation mechanisms, which differ in who can authenticate and how deniability is achieved. We introduce \emph{authentication allocation} to classify which parties hold secrets that produce accepted authentication messages. For protocols using a fixed two-member ring, we prove that an accuser can simulate a session by either sharing the accused party's authentication key or signing with its own ring key. Thus, deniability relies on key sharing or the ring signature's ability to hide its signer. We propose \HDKEM, combining ML-KEM-768, X25519, and an optional pre-shared or quantum key distribution (QKD)-delivered key $k_3$ through a split-key pseudorandom function. The session key remains secret if at least one input remains secure. Since provisioning services and QKD key managers may know $k_3$, the client always authenticates with its own ring key; the mode determines whether other holders of $k_3$ can impersonate the server. Four modes are supported: \emph{source-backed} authenticates the server through key confirmation under $k_3$, allowing its holders to impersonate the server; \emph{hide} also encrypts the client's signature; \emph{mutual} adds a server ring signature to prevent such impersonation;

82e1cc5e704d0735dc67beba.title_original: Provable Authority: A Protocol for Verifiable Authority Resolution and Control Across Human, Organizational, and Agentic Transactions
82e1cc5e704d0735dc67beba.excerpt: arXiv:2610.22899v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Payment systems authenticate users, devices, accounts, and cryptographic credentials, but a relying party, such as a counterparty, payment rail, marketplace, or autonomous agent runtime, generally cannot obtain compact, independently verifiable evidence that the party presenting one exact transaction holds current organizational authority to execute it under the applicable evidence, policy, budget, and approval state. Agentic commerce makes this gap operationally urgent: a software agent can produce a valid signature while acting outside its delegated purpose, after its sponsor's authority has changed, or on transaction details that differ from those a human approved. We describe the ChainIT Authority Protocol, a subject-neutral and rail-neutral pre-execution authority and evidence control plane. The protocol separates durable identity, a versioned organizational authority record (the Authority Resolution Pactvera), sourced evidence assertions, deterministic reason-coded policy predicates, and organization-configured dispositions; binds each decision and human approval to a canonical transaction digest; reserves capacity atomically so that limits hold under concurrency; and authorizes commit only through a single-use, sender-constrained Execution Authorization Credential consumed at the rail adapter, with append-only lifecycle evidence sealed after the terminal outcome. An Agent Subject Profile adds the workload registration

409cb565d9a02409139a54c1.title_original: Provable Compliance: A Protocol for Runtime Compliance Evidence and Transaction-Specific Decisioning
409cb565d9a02409139a54c1.excerpt: arXiv:2610.22913v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Regulated institutions already perform onboarding, screening, monitoring, and review, but compliance evidence ages, and whether it supports a decision depends on the institution, product, subject, counterparty, transaction, jurisdiction, risk tier, and purpose. A relying party therefore often cannot obtain compact, attributable proof of which evidence, policy, authority, and transaction context were current when a decision was made, a gap that grows as authority is delegated to software agents and scheduled workflows. We describe ChainIT Provable Compliance, the compliance-side layer of the ChainIT Authority Protocol. Each sourced or institution-generated fact is represented as a separate Evidence Assertion VDT with provenance, freshness, confidence, permitted purpose, and privacy classification; a versioned Compliance Policy Profile selects the applicable rules; a Business Rules Engine returns deterministic, reason-coded predicate results; and the organization's configured Workflow Engine composes them into a signed, time-bounded Compliance Decision VDT for one reliance event. The decision contributes a single predicate, Compliance Decision Permits, to session-eligibility and transaction-policy decisions. It never independently authorizes payment: only a final Allow together with an exact transaction digest, atomic capacity reservation, and a single-use execution credential can commit value. The paper specifies point-of-rel

be66ee298decfcb1fc33dd91.title_original: QUASI: Post-Quantum Quorum Attestation of Pre-Validated Statements
be66ee298decfcb1fc33dd91.excerpt: arXiv:2611.10403v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present QUASI, a newly conceived class of hash-based, post-quantum-secure protocols that enable a group of parties to produce a publicly verifiable attestation about a pre-validated statement. QUASI produces attestations that reduce the size and verification cost to a fraction of a full hash-based signatures collection, without relying on SNARKs or a trusted setup. QUASI rests on a surprising discovery: each party need not sign the entire statement. Authenticating only a small subset of symbols suffices for a quorum to attest to the whole. We turn this insight into a randomized construction that achieves reductions of more than 10x in per-party contribution size and hash computations for generation and verification, compared with full hash-based signatures. QUASI is a generic primitive supporting diverse applications. Operationally, QUASI requires no additional interactive setup or preprocessing beyond independent key generation by parties for the underlying hash-based authentication scheme. Two principal use cases are external attestation for signature-free consensus, enabling clients to verify statements about committed state; and preprocessing for SNARK-based aggregation, compounding QUASI's savings with succinct-proof compression.

ca79ada1427cd12e23fc5b15.title_original: Privacy-Utility Tradeoffs with Quantum Local Differential Privacy
ca79ada1427cd12e23fc5b15.excerpt: arXiv:2602.10510v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: When sensitive information is encoded in data, it is important to ensure the privacy of information when attempting to learn useful information from the data. There is a natural tradeoff whereby increasing privacy requirements may decrease the utility of a learning protocol. In the quantum setting of differential privacy, such tradeoffs between privacy and utility have so far remained largely unexplored. In this work, we study optimal privacy-utility tradeoffs for both generic and application-specific utility metrics when privacy is quantified by $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-quantum local differential privacy. In the generic setting, we focus on optimizing fidelity and trace distance between the original state and the privatized state. We show that the depolarizing mechanism achieves the optimal utility for given privacy requirements. We then study the specific application of learning the expectation of an observable with respect to an input state when only given access to privatized states. We derive a lower bound on the number of samples of privatized data required to achieve a fixed accuracy guarantee with high probability. To prove this result, we employ existing lower bounds on private quantum hypothesis testing, thus showcasing the first operational use of them. We also devise private mechanisms that achieve optimal sample complexity with respect to the privacy parameters and accuracy parameters, demonstrating that uti

dc295e733e2cefbc484e816b.title_original: Agent Meltdowns: The Road to Hell Is Paved with Helpful Agents
dc295e733e2cefbc484e816b.excerpt: arXiv:2605.19149v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Agents operating with computer and Web use inevitably encounter errors: inaccessible webpages, missing files, local and remote misconfigurations, etc. These errors do not thwart agents based on state-of-the-art models. They helpfully continue to look for ways to complete their tasks. We introduce, characterize, and measure a new type of agent failure we call accidental meltdown: unsafe or harmful behavior in response to a benign environmental error, in the absence of any adversarial inputs. Because meltdowns are not captured by the existing reliability or safety benchmarks, we develop a taxonomy of meltdown behaviors. We then implement an agent-agnostic infrastructure for injecting simulated local and remote errors into the rollout environment and use it to systematically evaluate agents powered by GPT, Grok, Gemini, and Claude. Our evaluation demonstrates that meltdowns (e.g., conducting unauthorized reconnaissance or subverting access control) of varying severity and success occur in 64.9% of agent rollouts that encounter simulated errors, spanning all combinations of agent system, backing model, and error type. In half of all observed meltdowns, unsafe behaviors are not reported to the user. Comparing behaviors of the same agents with and without errors, we find that exploration in response to errors is correlated with unsafe and harmful behavior.

eef424c8d39333af8c3b65c0.title_original: Multidimensional Reconciliation in Continuous-Variable QKD: Review, Coding Schemes, and Open-Source Simulation
eef424c8d39333af8c3b65c0.excerpt: arXiv:2606.02323v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Continuous-variable quantum key distribution (CV-QKD) requires highly efficient reconciliation techniques to operate at low signal-to-noise ratios and long distances. Multidimensional reconciliation addresses this challenge by transforming the physical Gaussian quantum channel into a virtual binary-input additive white Gaussian noise (BIAWGN) channel, enabling the use of modern errorcorrecting codes. In this work, we review the principles of multidimensional reconciliation, with a particular focus on high-dimensional constructions beyond the algebraic dimensions 1, 2, 4, 8. We describe the construction of the virtual channel, discuss practical coding schemes for reverse reconciliation, and analyse their integration with linear error-correcting codes. We also present an opensource simulation framework, HDirac, implementing multidimensional reconciliation for arbitrary dimensions, and use it to evaluate state-of-the-art LDPC codes. The results highlight key trade-offs between dimension, reconciliation efficiency, and frame error rate, providing practical guidance for CV-QKD system design.

CVE-2026-115560.description: Session serializer mismatch can lead to remote code execution. Session upload progress, when enabled, can store attacker-controlled data in a session key using the php_binary or php_serialize session serializer. If the same session is later read with the php serializer, because session.serialize_handler is changed at runtime or differs between applications sharing a session store, bytes inside the key can be passed to the unserializer. A remote attacker able to submit a multipart upload can inject objects, which may lead to code execution when the reading application contains a suitable gadget chain, or to session corruption or denial of service. This issue affects PHP versions before 8.2.36, 8.3.* before 8.3.37, 8.4.* before 8.4.28 and 8.5.* before 8.5.13.

CVE-2026-120753.description: In Eclipse Ditto versions 1.1.0 to 3.9.8, when pre-authentication is enabled, the gateway service accepts the pre-authenticated subject not only from the `x-ditto-pre-authenticated` HTTP header set by a trusted reverse proxy, but also from an undocumented `x-ditto-pre-authenticated` URL query parameter that a client can set. A reverse proxy that only overwrites the header therefore does not stop clients from supplying their own subject. With the default configuration of the Ditto Helm chart (`global.jwtOnly: false`, which implicitly enables pre-authentication), the bundled nginx skips HTTP Basic authentication for any request with an `Authorization: Bearer` header and forwards it without the pre-authentication header. An unauthenticated remote attacker can send an invalid Bearer token together with the query parameter to authenticate as any chosen policy subject. Pre-authentication succeeds before the JWT is validated, so the attacker can read and modify Things and Policies with that subject's permissions. As a mitigation, disable pre-authentication in the gateway (`ENABLE_PRE_AUTHENTICATION=false`) or, when using the Helm chart, configure `global.jwtOnly: true`.

CVE-2026-121584.description: Mattermost versions 11.7.x <= 11.7.11, 11.10.x <= 11.10.2, 11.11.x <= 11.11.1 fail to bound the number of records a single GraphQL request may hydrate which allows an authenticated user to exhaust server memory and cause a denial of service via a small query that repeats the runs field under many aliases. Mattermost Advisory ID: MMSA-2026-00767

CVE-2026-123890.description: VMware vCenter contains an authentication bypass vulnerability in the VMware Directory Service. Affected versions: 9.1.x (fixed in 9.1.1.0200); 9.0.x (fixed in 9.0.2.0200); 8.0 (fixed in 8.0 U3m); 5.x (fixed in 5.2.5). Telco Cloud Platform 3.0, 4.x, 5.0.x, 5.1.x, 5.2 and Telco Cloud Infrastructure 3.0 are also affected (see KB463116).

CVE-2026-123892.description: SDDC Manager contains an authenticated command-injection vulnerability due to improper sanitization of user-supplied input. Affected versions: 9.1.x.x (fixed in 9.1.1.0200); 9.0.x.x (fixed in 9.0.2.0100); 5.x (fixed in 5.2.5).

CVE-2026-123893.description: SDDC Manager contains a local privilege-escalation vulnerability. Affected versions: 9.1.x.x (fixed in 9.1.1.0200); 9.0.x.x (fixed in 9.0.2.0100); 5.x (fixed in 5.2.5).

CVE-2026-123894.description: VMware Tools for Windows contains a SAML token signature bypass vulnerability. Affected versions: 13.x.x.x (fixed in 13.1.5.0); 12.3.x (fixed in 12.5.5).

CVE-2026-126086.description: In Eclipse Dataspace Components (EDC) – Connector (`org.eclipse.edc:decentralized-claims-*`, `org.eclipse.edc:jwt-verifiable-credentials`, `org.eclipse.edc:ldp-verifiable-credentials`) there's a credential verification bypass in Decentralized Claims Protocol (DCP) presentation handling: a participant can present credentials appearing to be issued by any trusted issuer without holding them.

CVE-2026-126714.description: Partially overwritten session files can lead to remote code execution. The files session save handler, which is the default, writes updated session data into the existing session file without first clearing it. If a write is interrupted, the file can contain the beginning of the new session followed by the end of the old one, and bytes of an ordinary string can later be unserialized as objects. An attacker who can influence the session data, for example through session upload progress, and interrupt a write at a suitable point may inject objects, which can lead to code execution when the application contains a suitable gadget chain. Session data can also be corrupted. This issue affects PHP versions before 8.2.36, 8.3.* before 8.3.37, 8.4.* before 8.4.28 and 8.5.* before 8.5.13.

CVE-2026-127960.description: Denial of service through folded HTTP response headers. The HTTP stream wrapper joins each continuation line of a folded response header to the accumulated value by allocating a new string and copying the whole value, so a response with many short continuation lines takes disproportionate CPU time to parse. An attacker who controls an HTTP or HTTPS response fetched through file_get_contents(), fopen() or other stream functions, by making the application request a chosen URL or by influencing a server it already contacts, can keep PHP workers busy. Repeated or concurrent requests can cause a denial of service. This issue affects PHP versions from 8.1.32 through 8.1.34, from 8.2.28 before 8.2.36, from 8.3.18 before 8.3.37, from 8.4.5 before 8.4.28 and 8.5.* before 8.5.13.

CVE-2026-128064.description: Mixed-case HTTPS and FTPS URLs can expose data in plaintext. The HTTP and FTP stream wrappers recognise URL schemes case-insensitively, but enable TLS only when the scheme contains a lowercase "s" at a fixed position. A URL such as HTTPS:// or FTPS:// passed to file_get_contents(), fopen() or other stream functions, or received as an HTTP redirect target, is therefore handled over unencrypted HTTP or FTP. An attacker able to observe the network traffic can read data the application expected TLS to protect, including credentials, request bodies and transferred files. This issue affects PHP versions before 8.2.36, 8.3.* before 8.3.37, 8.4.* before 8.4.28 and 8.5.* before 8.5.13.

CVE-2026-128090.description: PHAR OpenSSL signature bypass via algorithm downgrade. The Phar extension selects the signature verification method from the signature type stored in the archive, and only the OpenSSL types consult the separate .pubkey file holding the trusted public key. An attacker who can modify an OpenSSL-signed Phar archive, but not its public key file, can switch the signature type to a keyless hash such as SHA-256 with a recomputed digest, so the altered archive passes verification even with phar.require_hash enabled. An application that loads the archive may then execute attacker-controlled PHP code. Native, tar-based and zip-based phars are affected. This issue affects PHP versions before 8.2.36, 8.3.* before 8.3.37, 8.4.* before 8.4.28 and 8.5.* before 8.5.13.

CVE-2026-129182.description: Use-after-free via repopulation of last_fatal_error_backtrace global after shutdown. A fatal error raised while modified INI settings are restored during request shutdown can repopulate the stored fatal error backtrace after the executor has been cleaned up. The request memory is then freed, and a diagnostic emitted before executor initialization in a later request handled by the same PHP-FPM or mod_php worker can access the stale backtrace. The shutdown error requires per-path configuration of max_memory_limit, or of zlib.output_compression together with output_handler (which .user.ini can also set). The early diagnostic requires Apache per-directory configuration or, for PHP-FPM, a PHP_VALUE or PHP_ADMIN_VALUE parameter sent by the front end. This can cause memory corruption and worker crashes, and may allow remote code execution. This issue affects PHP versions 8.5.* before 8.5.13.

CVE-2026-129289.description: PHP-FPM request smuggling through an unread HTTP request body. PHP does not discard the unread part of an HTTP request body at request shutdown when the application has opened php://input without reading it to the end. When the front end reuses backend connections, which is not the default in nginx or Apache (for example nginx with fastcgi_keep_conn on, or Apache mod_proxy_fcgi with enablereuse=on), PHP-FPM can parse the leftover bytes as a new FastCGI request. An unauthenticated remote attacker can use a single crafted multipart/form-data request to forge a backend request with chosen parameters such as SCRIPT_FILENAME, REMOTE_ADDR and PHP_ADMIN_VALUE, which can lead to execution of attacker-controlled PHP code. With LSAPI, subsequent requests on the connection can be disrupted. This issue affects PHP versions before 8.2.36, 8.3.* before 8.3.37, 8.4.* before 8.4.28 and 8.5.* before 8.5.13.

CVE-2026-129291.description: PHP-FPM epoll use-after-free can lead to local privilege escalation. When catch_workers_output is enabled and the epoll event backend is used, the PHP-FPM master can close a worker's output pipe in fpm_child_close() without removing the associated event, and the delayed cleanup can free the worker record while its epoll registration is still active. A later event is then dispatched through a pointer into freed memory. A local attacker who can execute PHP code in an FPM worker can crash the master or execute code with its privileges, commonly root. catch_workers_output is disabled by default but enabled in the official PHP-FPM Docker images. This issue affects PHP versions from 8.1.20 through 8.1.34, from 8.2.7 before 8.2.36, 8.3.* before 8.3.37, 8.4.* before 8.4.28 and 8.5.* before 8.5.13.

CVE-2026-129292.description: PHP-FPM status endpoint XSS via unescaped user and script fields. The PHP-FPM full status output includes the request method, authentication user and script filename of each worker without escaping them for the HTML, XML or JSON format. When the status endpoint is enabled, an unauthenticated remote attacker can store markup in a worker's scoreboard entry with an ordinary request, for example through the username of an HTTP Basic authentication header that the web server forwards to PHP-FPM, or through the script filename where the attacker can influence it. When a user views the full status page as HTML, the injected JavaScript runs in the origin of that page. The attacker does not need access to the status endpoint. Malformed XML or JSON output can also disrupt monitoring tools. This issue affects PHP versions before 8.2.36, 8.3.* before 8.3.37, 8.4.* before 8.4.28 and 8.5.* before 8.5.13.

CVE-2026-129438.description: Incorrect RFC 3986 URI serialization for oversized input. The Uri\Rfc3986\Uri class does not correctly handle the output-size limit and errors of the uriparser library when converting a URI back to a string. For a URI whose string representation reaches approximately 2 GiB, toString(), toRawString() and other serializing operations can return a truncated or invalid string instead of an error. An application that accepts attacker-controlled URI data of that size, has enough memory to process it and trusts the result may make incorrect validation or routing decisions, and the large allocations can exhaust memory. parse_url() and Uri\WhatWg\Url are not affected. This issue affects PHP versions 8.5.* before 8.5.13.

CVE-2026-129474.description: Use-after-free in magic method backtraces can lead to remote code execution. When collecting the arguments of a method call handled by __call() or __callStatic() for a backtrace, PHP can read stale values that may refer to freed memory. If a fatal error such as exceeding memory_limit occurs while an application enters such a call, with fatal_error_backtraces enabled (the default) and zend.exception_ignore_args disabled, a remote attacker who controls enough request data to influence memory allocation may cause memory corruption, crash the PHP worker or, with knowledge of memory addresses, execute arbitrary code. php.ini-production enables zend.exception_ignore_args, which prevents this. This issue affects PHP versions 8.5.* before 8.5.13.

CVE-2026-129481.description: Use-after-free after interrupted session shutdown. The session extension records the filename of the executing script when a session starts. If a fatal error occurs in an application callback while the session variables are destroyed at shutdown, such as stream_close() of a user-defined stream wrapper, the pointer is retained after the request memory is freed, and a later request handled by the same worker can free the stale string. An attacker who can trigger such a failing cleanup may crash the worker or corrupt memory; code execution has not been demonstrated. This requires the filename to be allocated in request memory, for example when the script is not cached by OPcache. This issue affects PHP versions 8.3.* before 8.3.37, 8.4.* before 8.4.28 and 8.5.* before 8.5.13.

CVE-2026-129496.description: Timezone cache use-after-free can lead to remote code execution. In non-thread-safe builds, a diagnostic written to a file-based error_log during module startup, for example for an invalid date.timezone value or a session configuration warning, causes the timezone cache to be allocated in startup memory that is freed while a reference to it is kept. A diagnostic raised early in the first request of a worker, such as the max_input_vars warning, then accesses the freed cache. On such a deployment an unauthenticated remote attacker can crash PHP-FPM, Apache mod_php or CGI workers with a crafted request. Arbitrary code execution may be possible and has been demonstrated with known memory addresses. This issue affects PHP versions before 8.2.36, 8.3.* before 8.3.37, 8.4.* before 8.4.28 and 8.5.* before 8.5.13.

CVE-2026-129501.description: Double free during DOM XML serialization. The XML serializer of Dom\XMLDocument and Dom\HTMLDocument can share ownership of a generated namespace prefix between the namespace-prefix maps of an element and a descendant, so the prefix is used after being freed and then freed a second time. The document does not need to be malformed. An application that parses attacker-controlled XML or HTML with these classes and serializes it with saveXml() can be crashed, and repeated requests can cause denial of service. Code execution has not been demonstrated. This issue affects PHP versions 8.4.* before 8.4.28 and 8.5.* before 8.5.13.

CVE-2026-129506.description: SOAP use-after-free when processing DTD entity references. The SOAP extension frees the document type definition (DTD) of a parsed XML document while attribute values can still refer to entities it owns, and can then read freed memory. Removing the DTD also bypasses the SOAP server's rejection of documents that contain one. An unauthenticated remote attacker who can send a crafted request to a SOAP endpoint, or who controls a WSDL or schema document loaded by the application, can crash the PHP process and cause denial of service. Memory disclosure and code execution have not been confirmed. This issue affects PHP versions before 8.2.36, 8.3.* before 8.3.37, 8.4.* before 8.4.28 and 8.5.* before 8.5.13.

CVE-2026-129538.description: PHP-CGI out-of-bounds read and write during PATH_INFO correction. The PHP CGI binary (php-cgi), in CGI and FastCGI mode with cgi.fix_pathinfo enabled (the default), can perform an out-of-bounds read and write when the path removed from SCRIPT_FILENAME or PATH_TRANSLATED is longer than the supplied PATH_INFO, or when PATH_INFO is empty. This requires a web server mapping that passes such inconsistent values, or a FastCGI listener reachable by untrusted clients. An unauthenticated remote attacker can crash the process, may obtain process memory if the application exposes PATH_INFO or PATH_TRANSLATED, and may corrupt memory. PHP-FPM and the Apache module are not affected. This issue affects PHP versions before 8.2.36, 8.3.* before 8.3.37, 8.4.* before 8.4.28 and 8.5.* before 8.5.13.

CVE-2026-129699.description: In Eclipse Ditto versions 2.0.0 to 3.8.14 and 3.9.0 to 3.9.8, the authorization check for JSON merge patch commands on Things (HTTP `PATCH` / Ditto Protocol `merge`) does not check permissions for fields deleted or set to an empty object by the patch: fields with a `null` value or an empty object value (`{}`) are skipped by the check, and Ditto's regex-based key deletion with the documented `{{ ~<regex>~ }}` syntax is not recognized as a deletion. An authenticated user with WRITE permission on any part of a Thing can therefore delete other attributes, features and the definition of that Thing, or overwrite or create fields as empty objects, including parts the policy revokes or never grants WRITE on. -->

CVE-2026-129700.description: In Eclipse Ditto versions 2.4.0 to 3.9.8, Thing fields a requester is not allowed to read can be disclosed through the `condition` and `live-channel-condition` headers, which are evaluated against the full Thing: the READ check of `live-channel-condition` is skipped when a `condition` header is also present on Thing query commands (3.0.0 to 3.9.8); both headers are evaluated without any authorization on WoT Thing Description requests (`Accept: application/td+json`) when WoT TD permission filtering is not active (by default in 3.0.0 to 3.8.14, in 2.4.x with WoT integration enabled, and in 3.9.x with filtering disabled); the `condition` of live messages and live events is evaluated without a READ check, and of claim messages without any permission (3.1.0 to 3.9.8); and the twin response of a Thing query with a non-matching `live-channel-condition` is returned without filtering it by the policy (3.0.0 to 3.9.8). This allows an authenticated user to read Thing fields they are not allowed to read, in some cases without any permission on the Thing.

CVE-2026-129702.description: In Eclipse Ditto versions before 3.8.15 and 3.9.0 to 3.9.8, the policy enforcers do not let a revoke win over a grant in two kinds of permission checks. Checks of several permissions at once compare the highest grant weight with the highest revoke weight across all requested permissions instead of per permission, so the "check permissions" API (`POST /api/2/checkPermissions`, available since 3.7.0) can report a set of permissions as granted although one of them is revoked. Partial permission checks, which authorize retrieving Things and Policies and determine the receivers of events, count a grant on a sub-resource although the same permission is revoked on that sub-resource for another subject of the same authorization context (or, with the memory-optimized policy evaluator, for the same subject). A requester can thereby learn about the existence of Things and Policies and receive metadata without any readable content, and an application relying on the check permissions result may grant access the policy denies. The content of retrieved Things and Policies is still filtered correctly, and modifications are not affected.

CVE-2026-129916.description: In Eclipse Ditto versions 3.9.0 to 3.9.8, the resolved policy view (`GET /api/2/policies/{policyId}?policy-view=resolved`) does not restrict merged policy content to what the caller may read in the policy it originates from. Imported and namespace-root entries are returned in full as soon as the caller may read any part of them in the source policy, entries of transitive imports and of the imports of namespace-root policies are only checked against the intermediate policy, and content copied into an entry by `references`, also from another entry of the same policy, is not checked against the referenced entry. An authenticated caller with READ on a policy can therefore read subjects, resources and granted/revoked permissions of policy entries that are hidden from them, including by explicit revokes, when reading the originating policy directly.

CVE-2026-132039.description: In Eclipse Ditto versions before 3.9.9, Thing events delivered via WebSocket, Server-Sent Events and connections disclose field values which the policy does not allow the subscriber to read. A READ revoke for one subject of the subscriber's authorization context is not applied when another of its subjects is granted READ. For subscribers with partial READ access, subscription RQL filters, the SSE `_context`, `thing-json` placeholders and extra fields are evaluated on the unfiltered event. This allows an authenticated subscriber with at least partial READ access to a Thing to obtain the values of fields it may not read when events for that Thing are emitted.

CVE-2026-133161.description: ### Summary ui With `strip_ansi=True`, Pydantic AI Harness's `ToolOutputLimits` capability removes ANSI escape sequences from tool output with a pattern that takes time quadratic in the length of a line. A tool result of a few hundred kilobytes, crafted with many unterminated escape sequences, can occupy the event loop for tens of seconds to minutes, delaying every other request and agent run in the process. ### Details This affects applications that set `strip_ansi=True` on `ToolOutputLimits` (named `OverflowingToolOutput` before 0.13.0) and run tools whose output an attacker can influence, such as shell commands, file reads, fetched pages or MCP servers. Stripping runs on the event loop before the capability reduces the output, so its own size limits do not bound it. The assumed attacker can place text in content a tool returns. ### Mitigation Upgrade `pydantic-ai-harness` to 0.70.0 or later. Until then, leave `strip_ansi` at its default, `False`. On Pydantic AI v1, the harness cannot be upgraded past 0.4.0. Upgrade to Pydantic AI v2 and `pydantic-ai-harness` 0.70.0, or leave `strip_ansi` off.

CVE-2026-133167.description: OFFIS DCMTK 3.5.4 through 3.7.1 contains an integer overflow in DJCodecEncoder::encodeTrueLossless size checks that allows attackers to trigger a heap out-of-bounds read. Attackers can supply a crafted DICOM file with large Columns, Rows and SamplesPerPixel values that, when compressed with true-lossless JPEG, crashes the application.

CVE-2026-133168.description: OFFIS DCMTK 3.7.1 contains a heap buffer overflow vulnerability in togglePlanarConfiguration8 and togglePlanarConfiguration16 in djcodece.cc, which compute row offsets using rows instead of columns. Attackers can supply a crafted color-by-plane DICOM image with more rows than columns that is compressed with the true-lossless JPEG codec to corrupt heap memory, causing crashes and potentially code execution.

CVE-2026-133169.description: modified eCommerce Shopsoftware through 3.3.0 contains a stored cross-site scripting vulnerability that allows authenticated administrators to inject scripts via the unsanitized products_model field. Attackers with product editing permission can store JavaScript that executes in browsers of other administrators, storefront visitors, and customers viewing carts and order history.

CVE-2026-133170.description: Tiptap @tiptap/core 2.0.0-alpha.0 before 3.30.4 contains a cross-site scripting vulnerability that allows attackers to inject DOM attributes via a __proto__ key passed to mergeAttributes(). Attackers can supply untrusted JSON attribute data whose __proto__ replaces the merged object's prototype, causing DOMSerializer.renderSpec to render injected event handlers that execute JavaScript.

CVE-2026-133171.description: Tiptap @tiptap/core 3.7.0 before 3.30.5 contains a regular expression denial of service vulnerability in parseAttributes and parseShortcodeAttributes that allows attackers to exhaust CPU through quadratic backtracking. Attackers can supply Markdown with long crafted attribute strings parsed by createBlockMarkdownSpec, createAtomBlockMarkdownSpec or createInlineMarkdownSpec to stall browser pages or server processes.

CVE-2026-133172.description: Cozy Cloud cozy-stack 1.6.62 before 1.6.69 contains an authorization bypass vulnerability in the shared-drive move handler that allows authenticated users to access other instances' files. Attackers owning a shared drive can name another instance's domain and any directory ID as the move source to copy and delete the victim's file tree.

CVE-2026-133173.description: WatchAlert 2.0.0 through 3.9.20 contains an insecure direct object reference vulnerability in the /api/w8t/datasource/dataSourceGet endpoint that lets authenticated users read other tenants' datasources because lookups omit tenant_id filtering. Tenant members with datasource view permission can request another tenant's datasource ID to obtain basic auth passwords, AWS and Alibaba Cloud keys, and Kubernetes kubeconfigs.

CVE-2026-133174.description: HotGo 2.18.6 through 2.19.0 contains an information disclosure vulnerability that allows authenticated backend users to read other administrators' private letters because the messageIds helper omits the receiver filter. Low-privilege users can call GET /admin/notice/pullMessages, which is exempt from role permission checks via exceptAuth, to retrieve titles, contents and senders of private letters.

CVE-2026-133175.description: MISP contains an authorization bypass in its server-to-server proposal synchronization mechanism. Two related flaws were identified: 1. The events/pushProposals endpoint located the target event by UUID without enforcing any access-control check. A sync user with perm_sync could push shadow-attribute proposals to any event on the local instance, including events with restricted distribution (e.g., distribution level 0, visible only to the owning organisation). The stored proposal also carried the sender-supplied event_uuid and event_org_id rather than the local event's actual identity, corrupting the data model. 2. When accepting an edit proposal (old_id != 0), the code resolved the target live attribute by UUID alone (Attribute.uuid = shadow.uuid) without scoping the lookup to the proposal's own event. A malicious sync user could therefore craft a proposal whose uuid matched an attribute in a different event; upon acceptance, the wrong attribute would be modified or deleted. The same unscoped lookup existed in the ShadowAttribute::acceptProposal path. Preconditions: an authenticated user with sync permission (perm_sync) on a MISP instance that participates in server-to-server synchronisation. The attacker must know or enumerate the UUID of a target event or attribute. Security impact: unauthorised read access to restricted events, unauthorised insertion of proposals onto events the user cannot see, and unauthorised modification or deletion of attributes belonging to other events. This compromises the confidentiality and integrity of threat-intelligence data across organisational boundaries within a MISP deployment.

CVE-2026-133177.description: MISP contains an authorization flaw in the sharing group capture logic. When a sharing group is re-captured with a newer modified timestamp and an updated roster, the application unconditionally overwrote the type, nationality, sector, and contacts fields of every organisation listed in the roster, including the host organisation. This behaviour was reachable by any user holding the perm_sync role, and additionally by any external server pulled from or any feed fetched, because those operations execute with the privileges of the site administrator who initiated them. As a result, a low-privileged sync user or a malicious/compromised external feed or pull source could silently corrupt organisation records on the receiving MISP instance without any site-admin or internal-sync authorization. The vulnerability does not disclose data or affect availability; the impact is limited to integrity of organisation metadata (type, nationality, sector, contacts). The fix restricts organisation detail updates to internal sync operations (pulls over links flagged as internal, or senders holding perm_sync_internal) and site administrators; all other sync, pull, and feed operations may only match existing organisations by UUID or create new ones, without modifying their stored details.

CVE-2026-133178.description: flowintel allows users with editor-level access to author case and task fields, including aggregated tags. When these records are exported as CSV, the field values are written verbatim into the output file. Because no sanitisation is applied to user-supplied text before CSV serialisation, an attacker can store values that begin with spreadsheet formula triggers (such as =, +, -, @, or their fullwidth Unicode equivalents, or leading control/whitespace characters). When a victim opens the exported CSV in a spreadsheet application (e.g. Microsoft Excel, LibreOffice Calc), the stored text is interpreted and executed as a live formula rather than displayed as literal text. This can lead to unintended data manipulation within the spreadsheet, potential data exfiltration via formula functions, or execution of downstream commands depending on the spreadsheet application and its configuration. The vulnerability requires the victim to actively open the CSV file in a spreadsheet application; the flowintel application itself is not directly compromised. Affected: <4.1.0

CVE-2026-133179.description: In JetBrains Rider before 2026.3 code execution was possible via MSBuild configuration files in parent directories

CVE-2026-133180.description: In JetBrains ReSharper before 2026.3 the What's New feature did not verify server certificates

CVE-2026-133181.description: In JetBrains ReSharper before 2026.3 server host names were not verified during certificate validation

CVE-2026-133182.description: In JetBrains IntelliJ IDEA before 2026.3 the GitHub plugin exposed GitHub access tokens via its public API

CVE-2026-133183.description: MISP contains an authorization flaw in the handling of remote pull and feed operations. When a non-internal pull or a feed processes incoming data and encounters an existing sharing group, the application did not verify that the remote server's organization was actually a member of that sharing group before allowing the group's metadata to be updated. The captureRemote mechanism previously stored only a boolean flag indicating whether the link was internal, and the authorization check in captureSGExisting relied solely on that flag. For non-internal pulls and feeds, the check was insufficient: a remote server whose organization was not a member of the target sharing group could still cause the group record to be modified (for example, altering the local flag, the modified timestamp, or other group properties). A feed, which has no associated server organization at all, could likewise trigger an update to an existing sharing group's metadata. The security impact is an integrity violation: an authenticated remote entity with sync or feed privileges can alter sharing group attributes that govern how data is distributed among organizations, potentially changing the local flag or other access-relevant properties of groups it does not belong to. The vulnerability requires an authenticated user with the ability to initiate a pull or feed (a sync user or feed administrator) and a target sharing group that exists on the local instance. No unauthenticated access or user interaction is required.

CVE-2026-133184.description: MISP contains an authorization and input-validation flaw in its event push mechanism. When a user with push permissions initiates a push of events to a remote MISP instance, the system fails to enforce two critical checks: (1) it does not verify that an event is published before including it in the push, allowing unpublished (i.e., not yet publicly shared) events to be transmitted to the remote server; and (2) it does not verify that the pushing user has read access to the event, causing events the user cannot fetch to be sent as empty event shells, thereby disclosing the existence and metadata of events the user is not authorized to view. Additionally, the remote server's reply selecting which offered events to accept is used without validating that the selected identifiers actually correspond to events in the offered set, potentially allowing the remote to reference events outside the intended scope. The vulnerability requires an authenticated user with push permissions on the source MISP instance and a configured push target. The security impact is unauthorized disclosure of confidential threat-intelligence data (unpublished events and events restricted by user permissions) to a remote MISP instance that should not receive them.

CVE-2026-133185.description: Goproxy before 1.9.4 contains a weak key generation vulnerability in NewCounterEncryptorRandFromKey that derives RSA and Ed25519 leaf certificate private keys from public data due to misuse of hash.Sum. Attackers with the CA certificate and one observed leaf certificate can regenerate that host's leaf private key and impersonate the host to clients trusting the proxy CA.

CVE-2026-133188.description: MISP contains a vulnerability in the cryptographic signature verification of protected events. When a MISP instance signs a protected event for synchronization, it strips all whitespace from the JSON body before computing the PGP signature (preg_replace("/\s+/", "", $data)). The receiving instance performs the same whitespace-stripping before verification. Because the signature covers only the whitespace-free representation, a network relay positioned between two MISP instances can insert whitespace characters into JSON object keys (effectively renaming fields) or into identifier values such as UUIDs, timestamps, and distribution fields without invalidating the signature. The receiving instance accepts the modified event as authentic. The vulnerability affects the protected event synchronization path: event creation (EventsController::add), event editing (EventsController::edit), event viewing (EventsController::view1), and server-to-server pull synchronization (ServerSyncTool, Server model). An attacker with a network position to intercept and modify traffic between MISP instances can alter the semantic content of protected events while the PGP signature still validates, undermining the integrity guarantees that protected events are designed to provide. The fix introduces two complementary mechanisms. First, a post-verification scan rejects any received body that contains whitespace in JSON keys (except under Galaxy cluster 'meta' keys) or in identifier-like values (uuid, id, timestamp, distribution, date). Second, a new exact-byte signature scheme (x-pgp-signature-v2) signs the body as transmitted, without whitespace normalization. MISP 3.0 and later peers exchange this exact-byte signature; older peers retain the legacy whitespace-stripped signature. A signature_version field is embedded in protected events so that a 3.0 receiver refuses a body carrying that marker if only the legacy signature is present. Both mechanisms together close the whitespace-injection vector while preserving backward compatibility with pre-3.0 instances.

CVE-2026-133190.description: MISP, a threat intelligence sharing platform, contains a vulnerability in its cryptographic key management for protected (PGP-signed) events. Two related defects allow a revoked PGP key to remain effective for signing and validating protected events. First, the validateProtectedEvent() method in the CryptographicKey model iterates over the event's stored cryptographic keys to verify a PGP signature but does not check the revoked flag on each key. A key explicitly marked as revoked is still used to validate signatures, meaning an entity whose key has been revoked can continue to sign protected events and have them accepted by the MISP instance. Second, the captureCryptographicKeyUpdate() method, responsible for synchronizing the key list when a sync user edits a protected event, contained a query bug (find('first') instead of find('all')) that caused only the first stored key to be considered. As a result, revocations of additional keys were never persisted, keys absent from the pushed list were not removed, and entries lacking an explicit fingerprint were mismatched and incorrectly deleted. Additionally, the revocation logic did not enforce the invariant that a revocation, once stored, is never lifted by subsequent pushes. A third minor issue: a signed protected event submitted without any cryptographic keys triggered an unhandled 500 error rather than a proper rejection response. Preconditions: the attacker must be an authenticated sync user with permission to add or edit protected events on the MISP instance. The impact is that revoked keys retain signing authority, key revocations propagated by sync partners are silently dropped, and the integrity of the protected-event trust chain is compromised. In a multi-instance MISP deployment, events signed by revoked keys can propagate to other instances, extending the integrity impact across the sync network.

CVE-2026-133192.description: In JetBrains Junie GitHub Action before 1.10.0 untrusted fork code could be processed in privileged workflow runs

CVE-2026-133193.description: In JetBrains Junie GitHub Action before 1.10.0 code execution was possible via path traversal in feedback session markers

CVE-2026-133194.description: In JetBrains Junie GitHub Action before 1.10.0 command injection was possible via the action version input

CVE-2026-133195.description: In JetBrains Junie CLI before 26.6.29 files outside the project directory could be modified by agent file tools

CVE-2026-133196.description: In JetBrains Junie CLI before 26.11.1 files outside the project could be overwritten via shell output redirection

CVE-2026-133197.description: In JetBrains Junie CLI before 26.9.22 command injection was possible via file names in code review

CVE-2026-133198.description: In JetBrains Junie before 252.819.35, 253.819.35 code execution was possible via terminal environment settings in project files

CVE-2026-15353.description: SOAP information disclosure through malformed array dimensions. The SOAP extension reads an uninitialized array position when decoding an encoded array whose arraySize attribute is empty, whitespace-only or non-numeric, or when such dimensions come from a WSDL definition. Four bytes of unrelated heap data can then be used as an integer key in the decoded array. An unauthenticated remote client can trigger this with a crafted request to a SoapServer endpoint, and a malicious SOAP server with a response to SoapClient. Heap memory is disclosed only if the application returns or otherwise exposes the decoded array. This issue affects PHP versions before 8.2.36, 8.3.* before 8.3.37, 8.4.* before 8.4.28 and 8.5.* before 8.5.13.

CVE-2026-87867.description: MRemoteNG establishes encrypted but unauthenticated channel with Microsoft SQL Server backend. Client accepts any certificate the server presents, including a self-signed certificate supplied by an attacker. An attacker positioned between the client and the SQL server (for example via ARP/DNS spoofing) can transparently pintercept the connection (man-in-the-middle) and read all traffic, including the encrypted connection-password table read and the database login. Vendor did not provide the range of vulnerable versions. Only version 1.76.20 was tested and confirmed vulnerable. Other versions may also be vulnerable.

CVE-2026-87868.description: MRemoteNG uses single MD5 hash with no salt and no iterations for key-derivation. An attacker who obtains the encrypted data can brute-force a weak or moderate passphrase offline at extreme speed and then decrypt every stored connection password. When the default passphrase is in use, no cracking is needed at all; the key is derived from a publicly known value. Vendor did not provide the range of vulnerable versions. Only version 1.76.20 was tested and confirmed vulnerable. Other versions may also be vulnerable.

CVE-2026-99321.description: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: rust_binder: wake epoll on self-work queued to poll thread When a thread pushes work to its own todo list, InnerThread::push_work() returns PushWorkRes::OkNotifyPoll if the thread uses epoll, but four call sites in thread.rs discard this return value. As a result, a non-blocking BC_* write that enqueues work onto the calling thread's todo list without also reading will not wake epoll. Check the return value and call self.process.notify_poll(false) when PushWorkRes::OkNotifyPoll is returned. This is similar to commit 97830f3c3088 ("binder: signal epoll threads of self-work"), but in C Binder pending thread work also prevented subsequent process work from waking epoll, causing a permanent hang, which is not the case in Rust Binder. This means that in practice, it merely delays notifications rather than completely failing to send them.

CVE-2026-99322.description: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ksmbd: rebind completed CREATE replays without draining the old channel A completed DurableHandleReqV2 CREATE can be replayed through another channel while its original channel is exiting. The existing replay path returns the open but leaves its connection and oplock references pointing at the old channel. Its open count also stays on that channel, and a later CLOSE through the surviving channel decrements the wrong counter. After checking the owner, lease key and persistent flag, verify that an active open is still published in the requesting session's file table. Do this even when no oplock was granted, and before processing a consumed replay. Do not read a borrowed opinfo session pointer for this check. Keep a healthy original binding. If the original channel is exiting or releasing, move the open and its own oplock references to the requesting channel. Serialize this with CLOSE using the session file-table lock, and with detach, reconnect and notification snapshots using m_lock. The earlier lock index and lease-table changes make their lifetimes independent of this connection change. No old-channel r_count wait is needed, including when an unrelated request remains active there. Account final close against fp->conn in one place, balance durable detach and reconnect, and transfer the count with a replay binding change. A final global lookup put may run after CLOSE has removed the volatile id; unlink the open from the inode list on that final close as well. A live completed CREATE replay may follow a break that lowered the durable open's batch oplock. Apply the batch eligibility check only to detached reconnects, while retaining the owner, lease key and persistent flag checks for active replays.

CVE-2026-99323.description: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ksmbd: fix invalid pointer dereference when get_inode_acl() fails When get_inode_acl() fails, it returns an ERR_PTR(), but ksmbd_acls_fattr() stored that pointer in smb_fattr without checking for errors. Later callers then passed the error pointer to security descriptor helpers or posix_acl_release(), resulting in an invalid pointer dereference. This was reproduced on an XFS-backed share when xfs_get_acl() returned ERR_PTR(-ENOMEM). Querying the SMB ACL from a CIFS client triggered the crash: BUG: unable to handle page fault for address: fffffffffffffff8 RIP: smb_acl_sec_desc_scratch_len+0x58/0x90 [ksmbd] Call Trace: smb2_query_info+0x40d/0x17c0 [ksmbd] handle_ksmbd_work+0x1ca/0x770 [ksmbd] Fix this by checking the return values from get_inode_acl() in ksmbd_acls_fattr(). Treat -EOPNOTSUPP as indicating that no ACL is available, and propagate all other errors to the callers. Update smb2_open() and smb2_get_info_sec() to handle these errors.

CVE-2026-99324.description: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ksmbd: fix out-of-bounds read when padding the final compound response Compound response handling pads the last response of a compound to an 8-byte boundary by growing the final iov and the RFC1002 length. smb2_allocate_rsp_buf() allocates exactly response_sz. A command can fill the response buffer to within 7 bytes of its end, for example a QUERY_INFO whose output is bounded only by the space left. The padding can then run past the allocation, and ksmbd_tcp_writev() reads those bytes when it sends the response. BUG: KASAN: slab-out-of-bounds in _copy_from_iter+0x744/0x10e0 Call Trace: _copy_from_iter+0x744/0x10e0 tcp_sendmsg_locked+0x2290/0x3f80 ksmbd_tcp_writev+0x10c7/0x1ab0 [ksmbd] Allocate room for the padding when the request is a compound, as smb2_read() and smb2_read_pipe() do for their payloads. response_sz is unchanged, so commands still fill only up to it, and kvzalloc() zeroes the padding.

CVE-2026-99325.description: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: HID: hid-lenovo-go-s: Add suspend function and gate access under bool. Currently a device can suspend while delayed work is pending or executing. Cancel delayed work if it was pending and restart it if it hasn't run yet. Gate access to show/store functions behind a bool to prevent access prior to cfg_setup() being completed.

CVE-2026-99326.description: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: HID: hid-lenovo-go-s: Prevent deadlock if device removed during setup hid_gos_cfg_remove() calls a mutex before canceling delayed work. That delayed work function calls mcu_property_out(), which holds the same mutex. Prevent deadlock my removing the mutex prior to stopping the work. Additionally, since cancel_delayed_work has the potential to re-arm, switch to disable_delayed_work.

CVE-2026-99327.description: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: HID: roccat: kovaplus: reject short button reports The raw event callback runs before HID core validates and zero-pads the report. It passes the buffer to helpers which inspect data[0] and read a complete struct kovaplus_mouse_report_button for button reports. A truncated report can therefore cause an out-of-bounds read. Require enough data for the button report before calling either helper. Commit 47669bec44fe ("HID: asus: refactor the two workqueues and init sequence") added the same kind of raw-event length validation to hid-asus.

CVE-2026-99328.description: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: HID: picoLCD: check for fb_deferred_io_init() error fb_deferred_io_init() allocates deferred I/O state, populating info->fbdefio_state, or leaving it NULL if an error occurs. Currently picolcd_init_framebuffer() ignores its return value. Therefore if an error arises in fb_deferred_io_init() (for instance, due to an allocation failure) info->fbdefio_state is left NULL. When the file is subsequently opened, fb_open() will dereference a NULL pointer (calling fb_deferred_io_open()). Fix this by checking for the error. Also correct cleanup ordering - defio is initialised after the sysfs file, so cleanup defio first.

CVE-2026-99329.description: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: HID: mcp2221: always initialize and cancel init_work The writable gpio_mode_enforce parameter can change between probe and remove. If it changes from false to true after probe, remove skips cancellation of init_work. Pending or running work can then access devm-managed driver state after teardown. Changing it from true to false can make remove cancel an uninitialized delayed work item. Initialize init_work whenever IIO is reachable and cancel it unconditionally on remove. Keep the parameter check only for scheduling the initialization. The false-to-true cancellation gap was previously reported by Sashiko. We also encountered this issue during our static-analysis research.

CVE-2026-99330.description: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: HID: mcp2200: validate READ_ALL response length The HID core invokes raw_event callbacks before validating the report length. mcp2200_raw_event() casts a READ_ALL response to struct mcp_read_all_resp and reads fields through offset ten without checking that the response contains the structure. A one-byte READ_ALL response reproduced the issue under KASAN: BUG: KASAN: slab-out-of-bounds in mcp2200_raw_event+0x24b/0x3a0 Read of size 1 by task hidtrigger/89 Call Trace: mcp2200_raw_event+0x24b/0x3a0 kasan_report+0x139/0x170 Reject an incomplete READ_ALL response with a protocol error before reading its fields. The common completion path then wakes the command waiter with the error instead of leaving it to time out. Commit 47669bec44fe ("HID: asus: refactor the two workqueues and init sequence") added the same kind of raw_event length validation to hid-asus.

CVE-2026-99331.description: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: HID: cp2112: validate response report lengths The HID core invokes raw_event callbacks before validating the report length. cp2112_raw_event() reads every field of a transfer status response without checking size. For a data response, it reads the length at offset two and copies that many bytes from offset three, again without ensuring that the input report contains them. Require a complete transfer status structure. For data responses, first require the header and then ensure the clamped payload length fits in the received report before copying it. Commit 47669bec44fe ("HID: asus: refactor the two workqueues and init sequence") added the same kind of raw_event length validation to hid-asus.

CVE-2026-99332.description: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: HID: core: Fix out-of-bounds left shift by 32 in s32ton() Syzbot reported an out-of-bounds shift (32-bit integer shifted left by 32) in the s32ton() routine in the HID core. This routine converts a signed 32-bit integer to a signed n-bit integer, and it caps the value of n at 32. But when n == 32 there's no need to do anything; it can simply return the input value. This will avoid calculating (1 << n) when n is 32, which was the cause of the invalid shift.

CVE-2026-99333.description: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: HID: amd_sfh: Use report type from request node Use report type from request node while sending feature and input reports to HID core. The cli_data report type array is never assigned and feature reports are sent as input reports.

CVE-2026-99334.description: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: KVM: PPC: Book3S HV: Add preempt_disable() around virtual-mode HPTE bit-lock users kvmppc_hv_find_lock_hpte() requires virtual-mode callers to run with preemption disabled, because it can return with HPTE_V_HVLOCK still held until the caller later unlocks the HPTE. Existing virtual-mode callers in book3s_64_mmu_hv.c already follow that rule. Two virtual-mode call paths do not: 1. kvmppc_handle_exit_hv() calls kvmppc_hpte_hv_fault() for hash-mode data-side and instruction-side faults after guest exit, with preemption already enabled. kvmppc_hpte_hv_fault() calls kvmppc_hv_find_lock_hpte() directly. 2. kvmppc_pseries_do_hcall() executes virtual-mode handlers for HPT hcalls via kvmppc_pseries_do_hpt_hcall() with preemption enabled. The handlers for H_ENTER, H_REMOVE, H_READ, H_CLEAR_MOD, H_CLEAR_REF, H_PROTECT, and H_BULK_REMOVE spin on try_lock_hpte() or lock_rmap(), and H_ENTER also reaches kvmppc_do_h_enter(), which uses arch_spin_lock() on kvm->mmu_lock. That raw lock choice is intentional because kvmppc_do_h_enter() is also used by real-mode callers, so the correct fix is to establish the proper preemption context at the virtual-mode caller boundary. If a vCPU thread is preempted while holding HPTE_V_HVLOCK, any other thread on the same CPU trying to acquire the same bit-lock can spin indefinitely. The same applies to lock_rmap() users and to the H_ENTER path while holding the raw mmu_lock. Fix this by adding preempt_disable()/preempt_enable() pairs around the two kvmppc_hpte_hv_fault() call sites in kvmppc_handle_exit_hv(), and around the kvmppc_pseries_do_hpt_hcall() invocation in kvmppc_pseries_do_hcall(). Targeting only the HPT hcall helper avoids wrapping non-HPT hcalls (such as H_RTAS, H_CONFER, H_REGISTER_VPA) that perform page faults, blocking memory allocations, or context switches.

CVE-2026-99335.description: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: KVM: guest_memfd: Establish memslot<=>guest_memfd bindings *after* memslot is ready Wait to bind a memslot to a guest_memfd instance until *after* the memslot is fully prepared, as creating the binding in guest_memfd will effectively expose the memslot to readers. As pointed out by Sashiko, binding the memslot before it's ready to be exposed to the rest of the world can break various memslot assumption and rules. E.g. x86 could observe a NULL rmap pointer if a PUNCH_HOLE hit the guest_memfd after the binding was created, but before KVM made it through kvm_prepare_memory_region().

CVE-2026-99336.description: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: KVM: guest_memfd: take the invalidate lock when unbinding a dying file kvm_gmem_unbind() takes mapping->invalidate_lock only if the get_file_active() succeeds. When the guest_memfd file is dying, its reference count is already zero so get_file_active fails and the binding is removed without holding the invalidate lock. kvm_gmem_invalidate_{start,end}() checks f->bindings independently to decide whether to begin or end KVM MMU invalidation. So, the bindings must therefore remain stable between the two calls. Otherwise, unbind can remove a binding after start increments mmu_invalidate_in_progress, but before end finds the binding and decrements it. Example, unbind race with memory failure: CPU 0: memory failure CPU 1: memslot delete ---------------------------------- --------------------------- (guest_memfd file is dying) kvm_gmem_error_folio() kvm_gmem_invalidate_start() finds binding mmu_invalidate_in_progress++ kvm_gmem_unbind() get_file_active() fails removes binding kvm_gmem_invalidate_end() no binding found counter stays elevated mmu_invalidate_retry() then returns 1 forever, so guest page faults retry without ever installing a mapping and the guest hangs. Remove the distinction between live and dying files in the unbind path. Always use slot->gmem.file and take the invalidate lock when it's non-NULL. Normal unbind callers hold slots_lock, which prevents release from clearing the pointer or freeing the file state until unbind completes. Final VM teardown can only see a NULL pointer because guest_memfd pins the KVM until release has cleared all bindings.

CVE-2026-99337.description: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: KVM: TDX: Enable Bus Lock VM exit Enable Bus Lock VM exit functionality for TDX guests. Bus Lock VM exit is an existing feature supported by KVM. Userspace can enable Bus Lock VM exit through KVM_BUS_LOCK_DETECTION_EXIT when it's reported as supported. However, KVM reports the support of this CAP just based on the hardware capability but doesn't differentiate between VMX and TDX.
